questions.scenario: A user is creating a quick password for a temporary guest account.
questions.hint: Look for common sequences that are the first thing attackers try.

candidates.explanation: This is one of the most common passwords globally and is cracked instantly by any tool.
While predictable, it is significantly stronger than a simple numeric sequence.
This password uses random characters, making it very strong against dictionary attacks.
A simple phrase is better than a short numeric sequence, though still vulnerable to dictionary attacks.

questions.scenario: A corporate employee is creating a password that must contain a capital letter, a number, and a symbol.
questions.hint: Attackers know exactly how people satisfy corporate complexity requirements.

candidates.explanation: Following the 'Word + Year + Symbol' pattern is extremely predictable and is a priority for cracking lists.
A random string of characters provides high entropy and no predictable pattern.
Long passphrases are very strong because length increases entropy more than complexity.
This is a strong, random sequence that avoids dictionary words.

questions.scenario: A developer believes that replacing letters with numbers (leetspeak) makes their password resistant to modern cracking tools.
questions.hint: Modern cracking tools automatically apply common character substitutions to every dictionary word.

candidates.explanation: Leetspeak (3 for e, 1 for i) is a known transformation. Combining it with a year and symbol is a common pattern.
This is a high-entropy string with no recognizable words or patterns.
Even without symbols, the length of this passphrase makes it mathematically very difficult to crack.
A random mix of characters and symbols provides strong resistance to dictionary attacks.
